utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then would you please prepare for the last, well, let's say, 20 minutes of today's session for -- to submit whatever you would like to submit in relation to the scheduling of future witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have sent it by e-mail and I will bring hard copies to the court next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could first the curtains be taken down. Could then the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break. We'll resume at 25 minutes past 1.00. Could everyone take care that preparations for re-starting are done a couple of minutes before that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although the curtains are down, we are in open session. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Once she's in, the curtains will be up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- could I address the Defence. Voice, low. Being seated. And consultations and discussions preferably during the breaks, and only, if necessary, during the hearing. And that means that immediately after we have taken a break, there ordinarily should be no need to be standing and to speak at a relatively high volume. Mr. Mladic may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Witness RM032. We'll wait until the curtains are up again. We still are in open session. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, before the break you mentioned an incident where a gentleman or a man had come and taken women away, and when he came for a second time to take the women away, the guard stopped him. If I may direct your attention to paragraph 47 of your statement. That's page 7 in the B/C/S, and it is between pages 6 and 7 of the English version. If I can ask you to look at that paragraph relating to Milenko Bjelica, is this the incident and the individual that you had talked about just prior to us taking the break? Have you had a chance to read this selection, madam, and is this the individual we talked -- that you talked about prior to us taking the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, whether that is the incident you talked about before the break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear no interpretation when you addressed me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the usher assist. Can you now hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Now I hear everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were invited to read paragraph 47, and you were then asked whether what is described in that paragraph is -- whether that's the same event you described before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. It is. That's the man we discussed before, the man who took those women to some farm, then brought them back, and then he wanted to take them out again but the policemen stopped him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that this person, Milenko Bjelica, was dressed in a different uniform than the police and soldiers that were guarding the Kalinovik school?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: I only remember he had this fuzzy, long Russian cap, the Russian cap, and he said himself that his name was Milenko Bjelica and that he was from Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did this individual come alone or with a group of people?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: He had several men with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that these several men had uniforms different from the police and soldiers that were watching the Kalinovik school?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: They wore --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure. This word may mean camouflage uniform and it can also be clothing of different colours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your last answer and describe a bit more in detail what kind of uniforms they were wearing or what kind of clothing they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember Marinko wore that cap. The others had multi-coloured clothes and also the green clothes from the previous army, the former army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, I would like to move to another incident. It's on the same page in the English, and it starts on the previous page in the B/C/S, at paragraph 46 of your statement. And it relates to the incident with Mr. Hasanbegovic. Am I correct that the individual --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that this individual that took out Mr. Hasanbegovic and referred to himself as Vojvoda, that he also had a different uniform or clothing than the police and soldiers that were guarding the school in Kalinovik?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: He wore black with a black kerchief around his neck. I don't remember now if he had a cap, but I remember this black kerchief around his neck and that wore black. He told us that he was a native of place number 12 and he lived in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did he come alone or with a group of his own men?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: There was several men with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that the men with him had different clothing than the guards at the Kalinovik school?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: I can't remember what they wore now. I remember only that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Am I correct that the guards guarding the Kalinovik school did not participate in this incident with Mr. Hasanbegovic?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: I don't think they did. Because he took Mr. Hasanbegovic away before. Hasanbegovic would come back black and blue, telling us that he had been beaten by that man. But the next time the man came, he took him again, and we were told all this by the women from upstairs, women from Kalinovik. We just heard two or three shots, and those women seemed to have seen that the man had a bloody knife, and Hasanbegovic never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could move on then. At paragraph 45 of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarifying question. In the statement, you say that Hasanbegovic was taken upstairs. Do I understand that, therefore, he remained within the building which was guarded by the policemen and the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, upstairs. We were on the ground floor, and there was another floor above us. So he was taken upstairs. That's where those women from Kalinovik were held, and they heard it all. And they saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You also said that: "A car arrived and women saw soldiers bringing down a body wrapped in a blanket." Are you positive about that they told you that it were soldiers that brought down that body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The women said that those were men who had come by that car. They brought the body down, wrapped in a blanket, and put it in the car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And whether these were soldiers or people belonging to a group that came in not being policemen or soldiers, that is, therefore, unclear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. The women who saw it with their own eyes probably saw that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But are you positive or are you not certain about whether they told that you soldiers - that is, men in uniform, the soldiers which guarded the school - or whether, perhaps, other men took the body downstairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were other men who brought down the body. They were not the guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can move then to paragraph 45 of your statement, and I believe that's on the same page in both versions. I want to ask you about these different groups of soldiers that were coming in. Am I correct that these men were dressed in different uniforms than the regular police and soldiers that were guarding the Kalinovik school?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: Yes. Because you could recognise policemen by their blue shirts. And there were others who wore the green uniform, the olive-green uniform. Those were the guards. But the other men who came in, they wore both the olive-green uniforms and camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that the regular police or soldiers that were guarding the school, they did not commit any of the acts that are listed in paragraph 45 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: I think that's right. I don't think these men did anything bad. I mean the policemen and the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Now if we could move to the seventh page in both versions of your statement, and I would direct your attention to paragraph 48. You talk about a visit to the Kalinovik school by the chief of police and the president of the SDS from Kalinovik. Do you have any better idea of the date when this may have occurred?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: I can't tell you. I can't -- I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. At the time that these persons visited, did you or anyone voice complaints to them about the acts or abuse performed by these visitors that we have talked about?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We complained to this man by the name of Govedarica and we complained to Zeljaja, but they said they couldn't do anything about it. We said that men were coming, taking us out, mistreating us, but they said, We can't help it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 49 of your statement - and that's still on the seventh page in both versions - you state: You "...did not see Mladic coming there." Does this mean that you did not see General Mladic ever at the school where you were being held?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: We never saw him, and nobody ever said he had visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that no officers of the army - that is to say, the army of the Republika Srpska - ever came to the Kalinovik school during the time period that you were there?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "officer." I said we had never seen Mr. Mladic, and we had never heard that he had visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My question to you, madam, was that with regards -- is it correct that nobody else who would say ever identified to be an officer of the Army of Republika Srpska ever visited the school in Kalinovik during the time-period that you were there?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: No. I mean they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At paragraph 44 of your statement, you talk about -- and that's on page 6 of the English and the B/C/S in e-court. You talk about losses of the Serbs at Rogoj on the battle-field. Did you hear any specifics about the number of casualties that were sustained?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you know or hear anything about bodies of Serb soldiers showing signs of mutilation or decapitation?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you know or hear anything about bodies of Serb soldiers showing signs of mutilation or decapitation? And I'm talking about in Rogoj.

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: I did not hear any of that. When Kunarac came, and when, once, I asked him why he had picked up children and taken them away, he said his family members had been killed at Trnovo and this was in retaliation. That's why he picked up those children.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could now focus on paragraphs 50 through 52 of your statement. That's page 7 in the English and I believe it should be page 7 of the B/C/S. This is where you're talking about the incident where the soldiers with long beards came and blindfolded you and took you to a hill to deliver a message to the Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: Yes. May I? It happened this way. One day Zeljaja and Govedarica came. One was chief of police, another was police commander. I don't know which was which. I confused these things. Anyway, they came one morning. They asked if there was anyone who could take a letter to the Muslim side where the Muslims were holding their line. I volunteered. My children started crying. I told them, Don't cry. If I don't come back, you still have an aunt and stay with her. They took me outside the school. There were men with long beards. I can't remember how many exactly there were in that group. They asked me if I had any more children. I said I had another two also there at the school, and they told me if I don't come back, my children would be killed. They blindfolded me with a white band and tied me, and I asked, Where are you taking me? And the -- this man cursed my mother and said, How dare you ask. They put me in a car. There was somebody else sitting next to me in the car. I don't know how many. They -- anyway, they took me to a hill, and that's where they had me get out of the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, my question was going to be about the -- the part that you just testified about with regard to Zeljaja and this Govedarica. Am I to understand from your testimony that both of these individuals -- am I to understand from your testimony that both of these individuals were affiliated with the police?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: Well, it's what they told us themselves, that one was chief of police and the other was police commander. I don't know which one was chief and which one was commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, madam. Am I correct at this time that there were no persons identified that were present -- that were identified as being officers of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything of that sort. No one provided me with such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're almost done. Now the place where you went and collected bodies of dead Serbs just before you were exchanged, do you have any idea of the approximate location? Are we talking about Rogoj, or are we talking about another location?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: It wasn't Rogoj. It was on the other side. Because that place was called Jakomislje. It's somewhere in Kalinovik. I don't know exactly. But that was the first time I went there. All I can remember is that it was called Jakomislje or Jakomistje [phoen]. I don't know the exact name but it was something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know if this was perhaps an incident -- strike that. I apologise. Did you ever hear of an incident involving civilians in an auto bus that were -- that were attacked and killed on the road Foca-Kalinovik in August of 1992? Serb civilians in an auto bus that were attacked by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: RM032
utterances.text: No, I wasn't in that area. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you announced that you would need another 20 minutes. We had a late start which was not due to the Chamber because we were waiting outside. Apparently the accused caused the late start. You've now taken almost 25 minutes. Are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am done with my questions. I was just going to thank the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the last question. Yes. Then, please, I give you an opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, I want to thank you for providing the answers, and I apologise if my questions were sometimes long, but I thank you for coming here and clarifying your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, any need for further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: None of the parties, neither the Bench has any further questions for you, Witness RM032. This concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague. It may not have been easy for you, but we'd like to thank you and we wish you a safe return home again. After the curtains are down, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can the witness -- can the curtains be pulled up again. The Chamber would like to provide guidance to the parties on its approach to Rule 92 ter decisions in this case, and do that first, and then have the administrative hearing. I already say that there are -- there's one slight change at the second page for transcribers and the interpreters who have been provided with a written version. In the past, the Chamber issued decisions on Prosecution Rule 92 ter motions, addressing Defence objections and deferring decisions on admission until all requirements of Rule 92 ter were met. The Defence often raises the same objections to Rule 92 ter motions. The Chamber considers that the parties have by now received sufficient guidance on the Chamber's approach in relation to many matters arising out of the Rule 92 ter litigation. Specifically, some of these matters are: 1. Requests for additional time for cross-examination; 2. Objections on the ground that the statements allegedly include expert evidence; 3. Objections because of references in statements to other testimony or documents not in evidence; 4. Objections to hearing a witness pursuant to Rule 92 ter due to the significance of the testimony; 5. Objections related to alleged violations of the Chamber's guidance on the presentation of evidence; 6. The procedure of appropriately redacting statements where the Prosecution does not rely on certain portions thereof or in view of the adjudicated facts. The Chamber invites the Defence to focus its objections on matters which have not been previously addressed by the Chamber or to specify why the Chamber's previous rulings do not address the Defence's specific concerns for the witness at stake. Similarly, the Prosecution is invited to exercise restraint in seeking leave to reply in relation to matters which have already been addressed many times by the Chamber. From now on, the Chamber will only issue decisions in relation to Rule 92 ter motions prior to the witness's testimony, if the filings raise an issue that has not been addressed sufficiently by the Chamber before, or if any specific issue warrants issuing a decision prior to the witness's appearance. Otherwise, the Chamber will decide on admission of proffered Rule 92 ter material when the witness appears in court. And this concludes the Chamber's guidance. Mr. Groome, we have ten minutes left, and the -- at least Judges have been provided with a draft dated the 3rd of September, 2012, confidential about witness scheduling. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So this draft was actually amended by me earlier today after I received estimates from Mr. Lukic for the witnesses in weeks 7, 8, and 9. There's not much to discuss here now. The Prosecution appreciates the Defence giving these estimates, and we will adjust the schedule so that we have approximately 17, 18 hours of hearing time for each week. If the Chamber in reviewing it believes that it -- it will intervene and change any of the times, the Prosecution, of course, would appreciate knowing that so we can adjust it accordingly. But I don't think there is any need for us to go witness by witness unless the Chamber would like to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, one observation, when I said a draft dated the 3rd of September, one second before I entered this courtroom, the one I had in my hands was taken out of my hands and replaced by one which was said the update of this morning by the Prosecution. So I take it that we have the one with the -- and we do see the cross-examination estimates in this draft. Mr. Lukic, would there be any matter you'd like to raise in relation to witness scheduling and, Mr. Groome, we are talking about weeks 7, also 8, no comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. So -- the -- I was hoping that we would have 7 through 10. Mr. Lukic was only able to get to 7 through 9. I would appreciate if in the coming week he could review the witnesses for week 10 and we will send another version with respect to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll do week 10 as soon as possible, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does that mean that at this very moment there's no further need to -- no further need to discuss scheduling?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Other than to say that I've already begun the process of adjusting the witnesses so there be some slight change in the witness order -- not the witness order but the number of witnesses per week, and I will make those corrections after we leave here today and I will send that later on today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We would have one question at this moment. Mr. Lukic, for the first few witnesses in week 7, the time for cross-examination exceeds what is usual there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any specific reason for that? And could you share your views with the Chamber on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first witness is an insider and he was convicted --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I just alert my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He is protected, RM066.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And his evidence will be provided in closed session, so perhaps we would use caution in even reference to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Let's then leave number 21 aside for a second and let's then focus on 22, where there are no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This gentleman gave his evidence in many trials in front of this Tribunal. So it's a huge amount of material that we have to review and probably discuss with him. As before, we will try to have time and cross less than we anticipate, but we have to be on a safe side and ask what we think should be needed to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I see that also the Prosecution has taken above average time for this 92 ter witness, which may to some extent also explain -- Could I, at the same time, urge the parties to the extent possible, to see whether they can seek agreements on matters. For example, we have often during the last days we have heard all kind of evidence elicited in cross-examination about, if I could say it short, skirmishes which have taken place in the area where the witness experienced what he testifies about, although having no personal knowledge of those skirmishes, and often such skirmishes or exchange of fire which has resulted in injuries or death of Serbs. Now, I can imagine that -- that these things happened and often not much more is said about, Do you know whether this happened or not. The witness says, Yeah, I heard about it, and has no further knowledge about it. I could imagine that the parties at some of these events could agree on that, that is what happened. It's not part of the indictment, so you might not go into the depth of that. We also understood that it's often background information rather than anything directly related to the charges. I would urge the parties to see whether we could be more efficient there, and I can imagine that often the Prosecution would not deny that such events were reported, including injuries and death of Serb soldiers or Serb civilians. So if that could be intensified that might save some time as well. We'll move very briefly into private session to see whether there's any further explanation as to Witness RM066. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Any other matter to be raised at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I also considered that this might be an opportunity, if the Defence had any issues to raise with respect to those witnesses that -- perhaps issues related to disclosure or other matters that we might productively resolve in the week adjournment. Best to be raised now. Of course, I realise Mr. Lukic may not have considered all of the issues with respect to these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this offer, but we'll contact the OTP tomorrow or in the coming week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because there are no further witnesses for this week, Mr. Groome, which means that there is no need to have a hearing tomorrow. Therefore, we adjourn until Monday, the 17th of September, at half past 9.00 in the morning in same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of September, 2012, at 9.30 a.m.
